sentences: Water runs beneath a sheer cliff, and a scholar lies stretched out on a rock above it.
This is A Lofty Scholar Gazing at Water, traditionally attributed to Kang Hui-an, a scholar-painter of the early Joseon dynasty.
The title says it all: a person of high mind, quietly looking at water.
The picture is tiny.
It is about twenty-three centimetres tall and less than sixteen wide, roughly the size of two open hands.
Yet nothing about it feels cramped.
Kang Hui-an passed the civil service examination in 1441, under King Sejong, and entered royal service.
King Sejong was his uncle by marriage, and he was admired for poetry, calligraphy and painting alike.
His handwriting is said to have served as a model for casting metal type.
He loved growing flowers and wrote a book on gardening, one of the earliest of its kind in Korea.
People called him a master of the three perfections: poetry, calligraphy and painting.
Now look at the scholar in the centre.
He lies on his stomach on a broad rock, his chin resting on his folded arms.
His gaze settles on the calm water below.
He is not fishing, reading or writing.
He is simply watching, and that is the whole point of the picture.
Look closely at his face.
His brow is high and bare, and a faint smile spreads across his lips.
He seems to be doing nothing at all, yet he is clearing his mind by watching the water.
In the old scholarly tradition, gazing at water was a way of reflecting on the self.
Now turn to the cliff behind him.
Vines hang down in long strands from the top, and the rocks are swept in with dark, rough ink.
Black stone and bare white paper push hard against each other.
The contrast gives the little picture a surprising force.
By comparison, the scholar's face and robe are drawn with only a few blunt, simple lines.
Rough nature and a gentle human figure meet on one small sheet.
Our eye is pulled back to the calm man at the centre again and again.
The painting places the figure large in the centre and reduces the landscape to a setting.
Compare it with An Gyeon's Dream Journey to the Peach Blossom Land from the same period, which unrolls a vast landscape seen from far away.
Here, instead, we are close enough to share the scholar's rock.
This kind of composition and its vigorous brushwork are seen as an early link to the Zhe school style of Ming China, which spread through Korean painting in the following century.
The picture is now in the collection of the National Museum of Korea in Seoul.
Step back and take in the whole sheet once more.
Then ask yourself a simple question.
When, today, did you last spend a few minutes doing nothing but looking, the way this scholar gazes at the water?
